commenti.body:
All indications are that the cut released to the cinemas was essentially Kubrick's final cut: 

>Writing for Vanity Fair, Kubrick collaborator Michael Herr recalled a phone call from the director regarding the cut that would be screened for the Warner Bros. executives four days before his death:  
  
... there was looping to be done and the music wasn't finished, lots of small technical fixes on color and sound; would I show work that wasn't finished? He had to show it to Tom and Nicole because they had to sign nudity releases, and to Terry Semel and Bob Daly of Warner Bros., but he hated it that he had to, and I could hear it in his voice that he did.

[https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eyes\_Wide\_Shut#Controversies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eyes_Wide_Shut#Controversies)

Links to Vanity Fair article on EWS by Michael Herr

[https://www.vanityfair.com/hollywood/2010/04/kubrick-199908](https://www.vanityfair.com/hollywood/2010/04/kubrick-199908)

So these inserts seem to be Kubrick's authorial intent. 

I think the most authoritative book on the subject is the following

Michel Chion Eyes Wide Shut. BFI Publishing (2002)

If you want to get into the weeds of this film this is the one. 

My personal feeling is that the cutaways to Bill's fantasy of the sailor screwing Alice are there not to make the story more clear, but to emphasise how pathetic Bill's cuckold obsession has become. 

Just put my take on EWS on letterboxd if you're interested.

[https://letterboxd.com/hootsmaguire/film/eyes-wide-shut/](https://letterboxd.com/hootsmaguire/film/eyes-wide-shut/)

Plane Impression has shown the evidence that it’s his final cut. What I’ll add to that is he hadn’t shown the movie for audiences at that point.  Both 2001 and The Shining got re-edited very close to release. 2001 lost about 12 minutes, mostly a full version of the second spacewalk, AFTER the premiere. The Shining had an epilogue removed so close to release that the actors in it are in the end credits. If Kubrick hadn’t died suddenly, he probably would‘ve made some tweaks to Eyes Wide Shut.

I've seen all this evidence , also that quote "I could hear it in his voice that he hated it" sounds like very much things were going to change. Those "last minute changes" can radically alter the thing you're making.

I agree about the purpose of Bill's fantasy but I think the way it's repeated is unnecessary. We know that that fantasy started his quest to begin with. Its repetition does not underline its significance but undermines it. It already is the note which his entire sexual misadventure is a war with. Besides, we have the scene with Nicole's dream to highlight. The repetitions seem excessive.

I would disagree that the repetition of the sailor fantasy is unnecessary, it's the very repetition that makes it so pathetic. There's also the opportunity each time to reflect on exactly what it says about Bill's psychology. 

For example, after he gets bothered by the gay-bashers with their slur, and after his inability to do the deed with Domino, I think it's the second repetition of the sequence, you might consider: "Is he projecting himself into Alice here? Does he want to be ravished by a hunky naval officer?"

It's unnecessary from a strict plot standpoint to repeat it, but I think there's more going on with those repetitions than plot mechanics. 

There is no way to determine anything about Kubrick's intention relating to this aspect, and many aspects, with any certainty, just as the film itself is a bundle of enigmas. The exact state of Kubrick's final concept for EWS is a known unknown, and will never be determined. We just have to work with what we've got.

Ideas and discussions are very interesting of course, but personally I would shy away from anything as objective-sounding as "evidence" on interpretations of EWS. My reading of it tends to go the other way, as a deliberate nexus of mystification and obfuscation based around Freudian concepts of the conflicting impulses of Eros ("good sex", sincere relations) and Thanatos ("abusive sex", power relations, consumerism).

I remember reading there was a child sacrifice scene that was cut out- where basically Tom cruises child was sacrificed infront of a whole party because he didn’t “fall in line”. The movie no doubt spawns a ton of conspiracy. I mean - he died before it was released - and they re edited it- seems a bit ironic given the context of the film if you think about it.

As I’m sure you know - the party scene was filmed (or Atleast the exterior) at a Rothschild property. People completely ignore this movie and what Kubrick was trying to say. He exposed them if you ask me. Them taking out the child sacrifice part may be easy to overlook as it can be dismissed as “it’s too extreme” but I think Kubrick was just trying to tell the truth.. as it’s probably closer to reality than just the girl wandering off in a book store at the end with two strangers watching her we saw previously at the party. 

There’s also the irony that Nicole Kidmans dad ended up being a part of a child trafficking ring. Want some more? This is all somewhat tied to epstein. Epstein (while he may enjoy being a pedo) also used children to help him black mail powerful entities - and I personally believe he was probably connected to the CIA - as they have historically implemented this method of black mailing before (watch The Godfather to get a better idea of how this works.. with the dead prostitute). “They” … basically just really powerful people who most of us don’t know- do control the media and can use it against a well known figure to destroy their reputation if needed. Kubrick is clearly a genius - and I believe eyes wide shut is somewhat of a expose of powerful people being tied to child trafficking/ sacrifice . And no … it’s not just one party. It’s probably democrats … republicans- who knows. But this goes back quite some time.

His movies are all very deep and eyes wide shut is the most disturbing IMO

But he was famous for changing stuff right until release, and sometimes even after release. It's probably really close to what it would have been, but he might have done a few additional edits.

I don't know if his perfectionism was always beneficial though. Some of the changes he made to some stuff seemed to obscure the meaning of certain scenes to me. Particularly on 2001.

Who can say although I've always felt like the final scene between Cruise and the physician needed to be edited down, as well as several other sequences where scenes go on too long. There are also some odd cuts here and there and one wonders if Kubrick, seeing how audiences responded, would have changed things around to make his message clearer. It's a certainly interesting film if somewhat minor, IMHO, in Kubrick's ouvre.

Of course we might argue and have an interesting exchange of opinions about what he did change in the last-minute cuts of released films before ***Eyes Wide Shut***. 

But any arguments about what would or wouldn't have been in the finished version of ***EWS*** are just speculation. Anyone's opinion is just as valid as anyone else's and there is no objective truth to be found on this issue. 

The 'text' we have is the one we have. That's it. It's what always happens when authors die and leave some work unfinsished.

But I don't really understand this characterization of it as pathetic.

Maybe I experience sexuality very differently than you or the average person but his reflection on that specific fantasy as presented in the film feels empathetic rather than fetishizing. Are you saying it's pathetic because of his inability to live up to his reflections on it? Also, the second repetition did not remotely make me think he wants to be ravished by a hunky naval officer, nor did any of the other repetitions. I can see how that would be a reading of it, but to me that's a reading of the film as a film rather than a world, and I think that's a childish way to watch great movies. To me, every encounter he has in the world is an attempt to square a personal, existential quest for truth and reality and, in a sense, immortality (I can fuck every woman forever, my sexuality is an endlessly unraveling relationship with the world) with a social existence that constantly reminds you your existential quest is vain and hopeless, or at least fleeting and shared with every other person - far too many to share a quest with.

Nicole's character's fantasy and the way she presents it is a coincidence of so many factors - a fight for truth, reality and mutual respect in a relationship which can instead become a fight for power, the way that fight for power is gendered, the way it's violent - you can tell from how she approaches that whole conversation that she knows that story / fantasy will translate a specific, fetishized way in Bill's head, and that she herself feels like a victim of that form of fetishization, unsure of how her sexuality exists outside of it. She also feels like she victimizes Bill through her awareness of and participation in these public sexual spectacles, their sex is performative but maybe not for each other. The entire movie feels to me like it takes place in the moments directly after she relates this fantasy to him, she makes him aware of the eyes of the entire species on their sex, something which, as a man, feeling himself territorial, private, invulnerable, he has felt he cannot afford to reflect on. The ending affirms their ability to fuck in their own room for only each other as the saving grace, the confirmation of an existence beyond the social and political. 

But again, I don't like that every time we're shown the sailor fantasy, it's Tom Cruise thinking, then the fantasy, then back to Tom thinking! I just keep thinking it would be stronger if the fantasy found its way back in moments where it's burning through the world, transitioning us from one scene to another. I just sort of don't believe he would be specifically thinking about that fantasy, because we're shown purposefully that he's being motivated by thought processes independent of that - he's shown to be thinking about the fantasy, then shown to have rather been dwelling on something else completely unrelated by what he does moments later. Do you think that's an intentional choice - to make us THINK Bill is fantasizing about Alice being fucked while he's clearly not? It feels like it's forcing us to consider that Bill is being motivated by this fantasy Alice shared even though it's already so obvious everything he does in the movie is motivated by the fantasy!

>I can see how that would be a reading of it, but to me that's a reading of the film as a film rather than a world, and I think that's a childish way to watch great movies.

Thanks for calling my reading of the film childish. It's a very constructive way to conduct a discussion, guaranteed to elicit a constructive response. Clearly nothing more I have to say about the film will be taken seriously, and further discussion is moot, as it's not the correct and mature way of watching films, that is 'as a world' and not 'as a film'.
